1.pericope_label: The disciples ask who is greatest; Christ sets a little child in the midst

schools.summary: Henry reads the dispute as a canvass for named places rather than for character, and apportions the offices each disciple expected, Peter lord-chancellor for holding the keys, Judas lord-treasurer for holding the bag, John as favourite, Andrew first called and so first preferred; the fault he traces to looking so much at the crown that they forgot the yoke and the cross.

Calvin finds it the sharpest instance of the flesh shaking off uneasiness, the prediction of the passion having made them sad while they fell to disputing the primacy as though they had tasted the nectar the poets feign, leaving what grieved them out of view and fixing on the resurrection. He names two faults, that they demanded repose and wages beforehand like soldiers who had served their time, and that they strove to excel each other instead of securing their brethren as large a share as themselves; and he supplies the definition of the humility required, which claims no merit before God, does not despise its brethren or aim to be thought above them, but reckons it enough to be one of the members and desires only that the Head be exalted.

Robertson reads the opening particle as pointing back to the tax-gatherers who had singled Peter out and concludes his primacy was not yet admitted, and notes the double negative shuts the disputants out of the kingdom altogether, let alone its big places. Ellicott adds the choice of the Three to the promise made to Peter and finds the less distinguished jealous while the sons of Zebedee conceded nothing; he warns against reading a later technical sense into the word for conversion, puts the weight on the warning that men disputing precedence showed they were not in the kingdom, and observes that to humble oneself in order to be great would reduce humility to hypocrisy. Lightfoot observes the ambitious dispute mostly followed the mention of Christ’s death, the dream of an earthly kingdom being sucked in with their first milk. Barnes reports from the parallels that they had disputed in the way and that Jesus perceived the thought of their heart, which he takes to imply omniscience.

Clarke takes the conversion required as deliverance from the national prejudice that looked for a temporal kingdom, and quotes Saady that infant hearts, free from avarice, care no more for a handful of silver than for a handful of dust.

Origen offers a third reading of the child, that the little one is the Holy Spirit, who humbled himself when called and was set in the midst of the disciples’ reason, so that men turned from all else are likened to the children God gave the Saviour.

Chrysostom notes the disciples were ashamed to show the feeling and so asked in general rather than why Peter had been honoured above them, and observes that the three distinguished at the transfiguration provoked no such grief as the singling out of one.

Jerome traces the question to the coin, the disciples having seen one piece of money pay for Peter and for the Lord and concluding from the equality of ransom that Peter was preferred; he gives two readings of the child, one whose tender age expresses the innocence they wanted and a deeper one in which Christ sets himself in the midst, and presses that the age is not enjoined but the innocence, which infants have by their years and the apostles must reach by striving. Hilary extends the name of little ones to all who believe through the hearing of faith, following their father, bearing no hate and trusting what they are told.

debates.question: What prompted the question about who is greatest?

positions.view: The tribute coin, whose single payment for Peter and the Lord implied Peter was preferred
Peter had been honoured above them, but shame made them ask in general terms
The tax-gatherers’ singling out of Peter, whose primacy was plainly not yet admitted
The choice of the Three together with the promise to Peter, which left the rest jealous
The mention of Christ’s death, which roused the dream of an earthly kingdom
Plain ambition, each disciple expecting a particular office of state

debates.question: Who or what is the little child set in the midst?

positions.view: A real child, whose tender age expresses the innocence they lacked; and deeper, Christ himself, come not to be ministered unto but to minister
The Holy Spirit, who humbled himself when called
All who believe through the hearing of faith

outliers.claim: Alone in taking the little one for the Holy Spirit rather than a child or a believer.
Alone in reading the contest as a canvass for named offices, assigning each disciple the post he expected.

5.pericope_label: Whoso receives one such little child receives Christ; the millstone and the sea

schools.summary: Henry makes the kindness Christ’s own, since whoever entertains a meek Christian keeps him in countenance and will not let him lose by his modesty, and the less the man is in himself the more the good will in it is to Christ. On the threat he observes that hell is worse than the depth of the sea, Jonah having found comfort in the deep where none ever had a grain of it in hell.

Calvin takes the saying for consolation lest humility seem troublesome, since by it Christ receives us under his protection and recommends us to the favour of men, the more a man abases himself the more highly to be honoured; on the offence he observes that a man who thinks too highly of himself must treat his brethren with disdain, and that the word forbids more than contempt alone, since he who gives himself no concern about the weak already withholds their due honour, the remedy being to stretch a hand to those the world despises. Gill reads the little one metaphorically, as one who is as this child for modesty and humility, free from pride and ambition and envy, so that the receiving is of Christ’s disciples into men’s houses or hearts, and takes a man offended when he is not received, his person despised and ministry rejected, until he drops his profession.

Barnes defines the offence as causing to fall or to sin, or putting anything in the way to hinder another’s piety, and concludes it were better for such a man to die before committing the sin; with Robertson he makes the millstone the larger stone turned by a beast and not the handmill, Robertson adding that the adjective meaning turned by an ass had no example outside the New Testament until the papyri supplied several, and glossing the deep as the sea of the sea. Lightfoot distinguishes it from the small mills used to grind spices for the wound of circumcision and takes the death for one perhaps never used among the Jews, named either to aggravate the thing or in allusion to the Dead Sea, where drowning implied devoting to execration. Ellicott agrees the Jewish law did not recognise it, reports it from the Greeks and from Augustus in cases of special infamy, cites Jerome for its practice in Galilee, and hears in the warning the thought rising unbidden in a Christ-like mind, which gazes on the innocent beauty of childhood and dreads to see it marred by evil.

Clarke agrees the term means a disciple only, the child having served above as the emblem of one, with Christ reckoning any kindness shown such a man for his sake as done to himself; and he bids those who act the part of the devil in tempting others hear the declaration and tremble. He cites the Scholiast on the Equites of Aristophanes and Suidas for the Greek practice of hanging a vast stone about the neck.

Origen begins simply, that a man who mortifies the lusts of manhood until he has a child’s condition is converted and the further he advances the greater he is; then he raises the difficulty himself and answers twice, first that not all converted with a view to the likeness have reached it, each wanting as much as he falls short of a child’s disposition, and then, against his own answer, that the perfect man may be the one called little, on the strength of the word that he who is least among you all is great and of Paul calling himself less than the least of saints.
Jerome is cited by Ellicott as the witness that drowning with a stone about the neck was practised in Galilee.

debates.question: Who is the little one whose reception is commended?

positions.view: A disciple, the child having served above only as the emblem of one
Any man who has mortified the lusts of manhood to a child’s condition, and perhaps the perfect man, apostle or bishop, who humbles himself among all that believe
The meek and humble Christian, whose entertainment Christ takes as done to himself

debates.question: Was drowning with a millstone a known penalty?

positions.view: A Greek practice, used by Augustus in cases of special infamy, and reported in Galilee
Perhaps never used among the Jews, the words naming it to aggravate the thing or in allusion to the Dead Sea
A Greek practice, on the authority of the Scholiast on Aristophanes and of Suidas

outliers.claim: Alone in allowing that the little one liable to offence may be the perfect man, an apostle or a bishop, rather than a weak believer.
Alone in setting hell against the depth of the sea by the case of Jonah, who had comfort in the deep.

7.pericope_label: Woe to the world because of offences; cut off the hand, foot and eye that offend

schools.summary: Henry turns the woe into a judicial principle, that he who opened the pit and kindled the fire was accountable for all the damage that ensued, so God’s making the sins of sinners serve his purposes will not secure them from his wrath.

Calvin makes the necessity God’s own purpose, who leaves his people exposed to exercise their faith and to separate believers, as the refuse and chaff, from the pure wheat; he sets out two constructions of the woe, a curse on the authors of offences, the world then meaning all unbelievers, or a lament over the evils he saw coming, and prefers the second, holding no plague more destructive. On the maiming he reaches the same severity as the moderns, that a man who hesitates to lose a limb spares it at the risk of eternal perdition.

Ellicott finds the clause and the woe uniting two truths in strange contrast, since crimes recur with something like the regularity of a law while in each instance the offender’s will was free and he is rightly held responsible. Barnes grounds the necessity in depravity, some always attempting to make others sin and rejoicing at success; he holds that attachments and employments not pursuable without sin must be abandoned however dear, denies the risen body will be maimed, and takes the eternal fire for conclusive proof that the sufferings of the wicked have no end. Robertson calls the two verses one of Matthew’s doublets, notes the first use in the Gospel of the word meaning ageless, and argues that making it an age-long fire must make the life age-long too, so that if the punishment is limited the life is shortened; the word for one-eyed he calls an Ionic compound the Atticists condemned and the vernacular revived.

Clarke reports that some eminent critics take the word of woe always to express sympathy in our Lord’s mouth, and adds that giver and taker of the offence are both exposed to ruin. Wesley puts the reader’s question and answers it, that this is a hard saying only if you take counsel with flesh and blood.

Origen applies the hand and eye to office in the congregations, so that when one who for his practical gifts bears the name of hand becomes a hand causing others to stumble, the eye is to say it has no need of him.

Chrysostom denies that the saying subverts free will, since the prophecy does not bring the offences in: it is not done because he foretold it, but he foretold it because it was certainly to come. He faces the objection that one who ought to stretch out a hand instead laments, and answers that nothing was left undone, so the lament falls on men nothing the better for that care; and the mourning is itself a kind of healing, since many whom advice did not profit amended when mourned for. Of the limbs he says it is not of the body’s limbs but of friends whom we esteem as limbs necessary to us, nothing being so hurtful as evil communications.

The Gloss offers the other account of the necessity, that offences must come because they are useful, that they which are approved may be made manifest. Raban fixes the word, scandal being Greek for a stumbling-block or fall, and a man scandalizing his brother who by word or deed amiss gives him occasion of falling. Jerome works the figure out, that if a man be united to thee as close as thy hand or eye, useful, anxious and quick to discern, and yet draw thee by the unmeetness of his behaviour toward hell, it is better to lack his kindred, and better to lead a solitary life than to lose eternal life for what this life needs.

debates.question: Why must offences come?

positions.view: Not by the prophecy’s compulsion; he foretold it because it was certainly to come
Because they are useful, that they which are approved may be made manifest
By human depravity, some always attempting to make others sin
By God’s own purpose, to exercise his people’s faith and separate chaff from wheat
Crimes recur with the regularity of a law, yet each offender’s will was free

debates.question: Is the woe a curse or a lament?

positions.view: A lament over coming evils; so some eminent critics read the word wherever our Lord uses it
A lament which is itself a kind of healing, since many whom advice did not profit amended when mourned for

debates.question: Do the hand, foot and eye mean limbs?

positions.view: Friends whom we esteem as limbs necessary to us
Officers in the congregation, named from their practical gifts
Attachments and employments which cannot be pursued without sin

debates.question: Does the eternal fire have an end?

positions.view: No; the phrase is conclusive proof that the sufferings of the wicked have no end
No; an age-long fire would make the life age-long too, so limiting the punishment shortens the life

outliers.claim: Alone in reading the hand and eye as named offices in the congregation rather than friends or besetting attachments.
Alone in arguing the duration of the punishment from the grammatical parallel with the duration of the life.

themes: it must needs be that offences come
the hand and the eye as friends

10.pericope_label: Despise not these little ones, whose angels behold the Father; the lost sheep sought

schools.summary: Henry takes a middle way on the angels, asking why we should suppose every saint has a guardian angel when every saint, as occasion requires, has a guard of them; and he reads the beholding of the face as prime ministers seeing the king’s, as if the strongest angels had charge of the weakest saints.

Clarke and Ellicott both find the belief in individual guardians established here, while Barnes denies the inference, holding that Christ does not mean every good man to have his own guardian, as many of the Jews believed, but that the angels are in general the guards of his followers; the beholding of the face Barnes reads from earthly courts, where free access marked favour. Robertson leaves both doors open, whether a special angel stands in that intimacy or the angels merely take an interest in God’s people. Ellicott keeps the scene in view, the child still there and perhaps folded in the arms of Jesus, and thinks some disciples’ faces betrayed the half-contemptuous wonder which drew the rebuke; on the verse that follows he reports the words wanting in many of the best manuscripts.

Clarke holds the Lord here establishes the notion received by almost all nations, that every person has a guardian angel with access to God for orders; and against Ellicott he counts five manuscripts, two versions and three fathers against the words of the following verse yet holds them authentic beyond doubt, the same sentence standing in the parallel place where no various reading has been found.

Chrysostom pairs the two commands, that above he bade them cut off the friendships of those who gave offence and here teaches honour to the saints, the perfect reckoned little ones because they seem poor and despicable. Cyril of Jerusalem qualifies the degree of the vision, that the angels behold God not as he is but as far as they are capable, Archangels more and Thrones and Dominions more still, yet all less than his worthiness, since with the Son only the Holy Spirit rightly beholds him.

Jerome reads the warning as tempering what went before, bidding us despise them not and next our own salvation seek to heal them, and exclaims that souls have high dignity, each having an angel set over it from birth. Augustine settles the last phrase, that the face of God means the manifestation of himself and not any feature of a body. Gregory reports from Dionysius that the lesser ranks are sent on this errand, the higher having no outward ministry, and resolves the difficulty by saying they come forth by a spiritual presence while keeping themselves by contemplation where they came from; he counts a hundred perfect, the Creator owning that number when he had made the substance of angels and men, and explains the greater joy by the righteous being often slothful through security while men with wicked deeds to remember glow with more heat in their love, as a general best loves the soldier who turns from flight and presses the foe. Hilary makes the angels carry up daily the prayers of those to be saved, so it is perilous to despise a man whose requests reach God by such a ministry; he takes the one sheep for one man and under him the whole human race, Christ the seeker, the ninety and nine the heavenly host he left. Bede grounds the joy differently, that there is greater matter for thanksgiving in man’s restoration than in the angels’ creation, since wonderfully are the angels made but more wonderfully man restored. Raban works the arithmetic, that nine wants one to make ten, and lost man was sought on earth so the number might be perfect in heaven.

debates.question: What are the angels of the little ones?

positions.view: A guardian angel for every person, as almost all nations have believed, with access to God for orders
The belief is distinctly recognised, and those set over the little ones are among the noblest, angels of the Presence
Not a guardian apiece, as many of the Jews believed, but the angels in general as guards of his followers
Either a special angel in that intimacy, or simply the angels’ interest in God’s people; the words decide neither
Not a guardian apiece but a guard of them as occasion requires, the strongest angels charged with the weakest saints
An angel set over each soul from its birth

debates.question: What does beholding the face of the Father mean?

positions.view: The manifestation of himself, not any feature of a body
As much as each order is capable of, Archangels more and Thrones and Dominions more still, yet all less than his worthiness
Free access, as at an earthly court, where it marked peculiar favour
The dignity of prime ministers, who see the king’s face

debates.question: Is the verse on the Son of man coming to save the lost genuine?

positions.view: Wanting in many of the best manuscripts
Authentic beyond doubt, despite five manuscripts, two versions and three fathers against it, since the same sentence stands in the parallel place with no various reading

debates.question: Why is there more joy over the one sheep found?

positions.view: The righteous are often slothful through security, while men with wicked deeds to remember love with more heat
There is greater matter for thanksgiving in man’s restoration than in the angels’ creation
Because the number must be made perfect in heaven, nine wanting one to make ten

outliers.claim: Alone in limiting the angelic vision by rank, so that the beholding is partial even for Thrones and Dominions.
Alone in explaining the greater joy by the slothfulness of the secure rather than by the worth of what was restored.

themes: the Son of man come to save

15.pericope_label: Tell him his fault between thee and him alone; then witnesses; then the church

schools.summary: Henry gives the practical reason for the privacy, that to convince a man you must not expose him, which only exasperates and makes the reproof look like revenge; and he observes that great sins amuse and silence conscience, since David’s heart smote him for Saul’s skirt and for numbering the people but not for Uriah till Nathan said, Thou art the man.

Ellicott observes the word for church recurs here and only here after the promise to Peter, and holds the true rendering to be congregation, as every English version from Tyndale had it until the Rhemish translators brought in church, so the appeal is to the society itself and not its rulers, and a man who defies its judgment practically excommunicates himself; he refuses to let the Pharisees’ treatment of the heathen stand as the pattern, such men being still men and entitled to courtesy and all kindly offices. Barnes allows either the whole assembly or those authorized to try such cases, noting the synagogue’s bench of elders, and holds that religious intercourse ceases but not kindness or aid in affliction, owed to all men. Robertson takes it for the local body, not the general, and asks whether an actual assembly is meant or the churches organized later. Lightfoot declines the long dispute and shifts the ground, holding the business to be less the censure of the sinner than the vindication of the reprover, since the witnesses could not testify to a sin they knew nothing of but could testify that due reproof was used.
Clarke would lay the matter before the congregation of the place, or the minister and elders as its representatives.

Origen states the hardest question and refuses both answers: one man, looking to infinite mercy, says the words distinguish no sins, another that they cannot cover the great sins, a man guilty of those being not a brother but only called one; yet the first encourages the careless and the second too great severity, since we cannot decide that a man finally perishes, and he who is thrice told may hearken the fourth time.

Chrysostom notes that the Lord, having terrified those who give offence, now checks the opposite fault in those who take it, the grieved man being drawn to his grievers because the wrongdoer will not readily come for shame; he marks the choice of words, not Accuse him nor Demand redress but Tell him his fault, since a man held down by anger or shame is stupefied as in deep slumber and the one in his right senses must go to the one in the disease.

Augustine makes the privacy follow from the offence, that if you alone know the trespass and rebuke him before all you do not correct but betray him, so faults done before all are rebuked before all and those done in private in private, by which rule the Scriptures are consistent; he adds that the rebuke should be in love, not eager to wound but anxious to amend, warns that a man who passes the fault by becomes the worse of the two, and insists that while such a man is no longer reckoned among the brethren his salvation is not to be neglected, since we do not number the heathen among the brethren yet always seek theirs. Jerome distinguishes the wrong done to us, which we must forgive, from that done to God, which is not ours to decide, and observes that we do the contrary, merciful where God is affronted and prosecuting where we are. Raban guards the other side, that forgiveness is not commanded indiscriminately but toward him who will hearken and do penitence, so it is neither unattainable nor too far relaxed. The Gloss makes excommunication follow, pronounced by the Church’s mouth through the priest, the whole Church working in him.

debates.question: Why must the reproof be private first?

positions.view: Because the offence was private; to rebuke before all what you alone know is to betray and not correct
Because the wrongdoer will not come for shame, so the grieved must go to him
Because exposing a man exasperates him and makes the reproof look like revenge

debates.question: What is the church that must be told?

positions.view: The congregation itself and not its rulers, as every English version from Tyndale had it until the Rhemish translators
Either the whole assembly or those authorized to try such cases, on the synagogue’s model
The congregation of the place, or the minister and elders as its representatives
The local body and not the general; whether an actual assembly or the later organized churches is left open

debates.question: Do these words cover great sins as well as small?

positions.view: Neither answer will do: unlimited forgiveness encourages the careless, and excluding great sins brings in too great severity
Forgiveness is commanded toward him who will hearken and do penitence, not indiscriminately
The wrong done to us we must forgive; the wrong done to God is not ours to decide

debates.question: How is the excommunicate to be treated?

positions.view: His salvation is not to be neglected, since we always seek the heathen’s too
Religious intercourse ceases, but not kindness or aid in affliction, owed to all men
Not on the Pharisees’ pattern; such men are still men, entitled to courtesy and all kindly offices

outliers.claim: Alone in making the procedure chiefly the vindication of the reprover rather than the censure of the sinner, since the witnesses can attest only that due reproof was used.

themes: as a heathen and a publican

18.pericope_label: Whatsoever ye bind on earth is bound in heaven; where two or three are gathered

schools.summary: Henry qualifies the ratification, that ministers are owned while they adhere to Christ’s laws, the key not turning the wrong way; he will not have them judges and lords, the saying being not that what they decree shall be done but what they agree to ask of God, and he urges that no sentence be passed which cannot in faith be asked of God to confirm.

Barnes draws the deity of Christ from the last clause by enumeration, that at one hour two or three are assembled in every city across the world with Jesus in the midst of them all, which is impossible unless he be God. Lightfoot takes the fuller sense of the authority, to bind and loose anything that seemed the apostles good under the Spirit’s guidance, and claims none but the apostles was ever led into all truth, they alone delivering a rule of faith to the church.

Clarke reports that Christian interpreters generally restrain the words to discipline and authority, and argues against them from the Mishna and later rabbins, where binding declares a thing unlawful and loosing lawful; the pronouns are neuter in both places, whatsoever thing and not whosoever, so the words are of things and not persons, an interpretation he credits to Lightfoot, quoting the formula by which the Jews set a man apart to teach, take thou liberty to teach what is bound and what is loose. He sets beside the last clause the rabbinic saying that wherever even two sit in discourse concerning the law the divine presence is among them, and presses the argument that none but God could say these words with truth, since God alone is everywhere present.

Origen reads one word closely, that Christ says in heaven and not, as to Peter, in the heavens, the rest not having yet attained the like perfection; and on the gathering he says Christ does not say he will be but that he is in the midst, since as soon as they agree he is among them, explaining the failure of prayer by the want of that agreement, in doctrine and life alike, for as in music, unless the voices are in time there is no pleasure to the hearer, so in the Church, unless united, God is not pleased.

Chrysostom marks who is not addressed, that it is not said to the Church’s head, Bind such a man, but if you shall bind him the bonds shall be indissoluble, the thing left to discretion; he sets the incorrigible under a twofold necessity, the casting out here and the binding in heaven, and gives four reasons why agreeing men do not obtain, that they ask what is not expedient, bring not their own part, pray seeking vengeance, and seek mercy for sinners who have not repented. He fixes the condition of the promise, that it is not said barely where they are gathered but in my name.

Jerome explains why the promise follows the sentence, that the brother so contemned might answer, if you despise me I will despise you, so the power is conferred that the apostles may be sure man’s sentence is ratified by God’s. Augustine adds the condition, that when you hold a man as a publican you bind him on earth but must bind with just cause, an unjust cause breaking rightful bonds, and when you have corrected and agreed with him you have loosed him, conferring the boon not on yourself but on him. The Gloss widens the ratification from excommunication to every petition offered by men holding together in the Church’s unity.

debates.question: Are binding and loosing spoken of things or of persons?

positions.view: Of things: the pronouns are neuter, and the rabbins use the words to declare a thing lawful or unlawful
Of persons, in discipline: the incorrigible is cast out here and bound in heaven

debates.question: On what condition does heaven ratify the sentence?

positions.view: On a just cause; an unjust cause breaks rightful bonds
While ministers adhere to Christ’s laws, the key not turning the wrong way
The thing is left to discretion, the Lord not naming whom to bind

debates.question: Why do agreeing petitioners sometimes fail to obtain?

positions.view: Four causes: asking what is not expedient, not bringing their own part, seeking vengeance, seeking mercy for the unrepentant
Want of real agreement, in doctrine and in life, as voices out of time give no pleasure

debates.question: Does the promise of presence prove Christ’s deity?

positions.view: Yes; none but God could say it with truth, since God alone is everywhere present
Yes; two or three are assembled in every city at one hour, impossible unless he be God
The clause is conditional on being gathered in his name, not merely gathered

outliers.claim: Alone with Lightfoot against the general run of Christian interpreters in making the words declare things lawful or unlawful rather than bind and loose persons.
Alone in resting a distinction on the singular heaven here against the plural spoken to Peter.

themes: there am I in the midst

21.pericope_label: Peter asks how oft he must forgive; until seventy times seven

schools.summary: Henry is sharpest on the keeping of count, finding ill-nature in scoring up the injuries we forgive, as if we would allow ourselves revenge when the measure is full, for God keeps account, being the Judge, and we must not, lest we step into his throne.

Calvin finds the objection natural to the flesh, that if we forgive so readily our lenity will induce others to offend us, and observes that Christ, far from yielding, declares expressly there ought to be no limit.

Lightfoot measures the question against the schools, which forbade a wronged man to be difficult to pardon, that not being the manner of the seed of Israel, and praised the readiest to forgive, but he finds a snake under it, for they pardoned once, twice, thrice, and the fourth time they did not. Barnes reports the same limit of three times and no fourth, so that Peter more than doubled the received charity. Ellicott thinks the sacred number suggested itself as the natural limit, perhaps with a half-conscious memory of the prophet, that for three transgressions and four the punishment should not turn away; he holds the symbolic numbers designed to lead the questioner from any numerical standard, since as there is no limit to God’s forgiveness there should be none to man’s. Robertson quotes Plummer, that a man who asks such a question does not know what forgiveness means, grants it is unclear whether the idiom means seventy-seven or four hundred and ninety, notes the same ambiguity in the Greek of Genesis, and says it matters little since unlimited forgiveness is meant either way.

Clarke reports the limit as three times and no fourth, and sets the words beside the boast of Lamech, where the same phrase is used of vengeance, turning the sum on the reader: let a man search ever so accurately and he will not find four hundred and ninety such offences in his whole life, an offence properly so called being given wantonly, without provocation. Wesley answers in a line, as often as there is occasion, a certain number put for an uncertain.

Origen refuses the literal reckoning as silly and unworthy both of Peter’s progress and the divine magnanimity of Jesus, offering instead that six denotes toil and seven repose, so pardon belongs to brethren who sin in things of this world.

Chrysostom denies that any number is set, holding no limit is set but something endless and ever enduring; in his homily he supplies Peter’s reasoning, that for the unrepentant a limit was fixed by the words about the heathen and the publican, but for him who is told his fault and repents none has been given.

Jerome traces the question to what went before, the warning against despising the little ones and the rule for a brother who sins, and takes the larger figure of four hundred and ninety. Augustine takes the smaller and reads it symbolically, the law signified by ten and sin by eleven because it passes the denary line, while seven stands for a whole since time goes round in seven days, eleven taken seven times yielding the number; yet he will not stop at any figure, bidding us forgive a man who sins seventy-eight times, and a hundred, and however often, for if Christ found a thousand sins and forgave all we are not to withdraw our forgiveness. Raban distinguishes two pardons, one to a brother who seeks it that he may live with us in social charity, as Joseph to his brethren, and one to a hostile foe that we may wish him good, as David mourning Saul.

debates.question: Is the answer a number at all?

positions.view: No; no limit is set but something endless and ever enduring
No; the symbolic numbers are designed to lead the questioner away from any numerical standard
A certain number put for an uncertain, meaning as often as there is occasion
No limit whatever; Christ, far from yielding to the objection, declares expressly there ought to be none
No figure will do; forgive seventy-eight times, and a hundred, and however often

debates.question: Does the idiom mean seventy-seven or four hundred and ninety?

positions.view: Four hundred and ninety
Seventy-seven, read symbolically as eleven taken seven times
Unclear, and it matters little, since unlimited forgiveness is meant either way

debates.question: Why did Peter propose seven times?

positions.view: Against the schools’ limit of three and no fourth, so he more than doubled the received charity
The sacred number suggested itself as the natural limit
Self-stinting; and there is ill-nature in scoring up the injuries we forgive at all
The literal reckoning is silly and unworthy of Peter’s progress; six denotes toil and seven repose

outliers.claim: Alone in turning the arithmetic on the reader, that no man will find he has received four hundred and ninety unprovoked offences in a whole life.
Alone in dividing the duty into two pardons, one to the brother who asks and one to the foe who does not.

themes: the schools’ three and no fourth
seventy-seven or four hundred and ninety

23.pericope_label: A king takes account of his servants; one owing ten thousand talents is forgiven

schools.summary: Henry adds a fifth valuation of the debt, one million eight hundred and seventy-five thousand pounds, and makes conscience the auditor that, unless bribed, will not write fifty for a hundred; the scripture concluding all under sin he calls a statute of bankruptcy against us all.

Calvin says the doctrine needed confirming because it is hard to bend us to mercy and we weary quickly in bearing many faults of brethren, and that those who will not pardon judge very ill for themselves, subjecting themselves to a law equally stern; he rests the likeness on three contrasts, king against servant, large sum against ordinary, extraordinary kindness against extreme cruelty. Gill reads the kingdom of the Gospel church state, turns the insolvency into doctrine, that a debt of sin cannot be discharged by a debt of obedience, God having a prior right to the latter, and sin against an infinite God contracting an infinite debt no creature can pay, and insists the motive of the remission lay in the king’s own goodness and not in anything the man said or did.

Barnes makes the talent three thousand shekels and the whole sixteen million dollars, guesses the servants collectors of revenue since kings farmed out a province’s taxes, grounds the selling in the law, and warns against pressing that clause, thrown in to keep the story consistent and explain the servant’s anxiety for delay. Ellicott, from the Greek translators’ use of the word for the Hebrew weight, gets two and a half million, draws the lesson from the disagreement itself that the sum is named in its vague vastness, and will not grant the plea much, calling the promise an idle boast which yet aptly describes the first impulse of one roused to a sense of sin, who tries to balance the account by instalments and seeks to be justified by works until the compassion meets him with more than he asked. Robertson reckons a thousand dollars the talent and notes the imperial taxes of Judea, Idumea, and Samaria came to six hundred a year.

Clarke calls the sum a myriad, the highest number in Greek notation, worth four and a half million sterling in silver or sixty-seven and a half in gold, equal to the annual revenue of the British empire, and reaches the tributary prince by arithmetic, no hired servant being able to owe such a sum. Wesley says the figure intimates the weight of our offences and our incapacity of satisfying God.

Origen takes the kingdom of heaven to be the Son himself, who as he is wisdom and righteousness and truth is also a kingdom, not of things beneath but of all above, reigning in every thought of the man no longer under sin’s reign, so that the reckoning is his return at the consummation.
Chrysostom reads the parable as a guard on the command just given, lest any think the Lord had enjoined something burdensome in requiring endless pardon.

Jerome notes the Syrian custom of adding a parable, so that what a bare precept cannot hold may be held by example. Augustine finds the figure in the law, that it is set forth in ten precepts, so ten thousand talents denote all sins doable under it, the hundred denarii keeping that number, a hundred hundreds being ten thousand and ten tens a hundred. Remigius takes the kingdom for the holy Church, in which the Lord reckons with those he has set over it. Raban reads the debtor allegorically as the people bound to the ten commandments.

debates.question: What is the kingdom likened to a king?

positions.view: The Son himself, who as wisdom and righteousness and truth is also a kingdom
The holy Church, in which the Lord reckons with those set over it
The Gospel church state and the methods of God’s dealings in it

debates.question: How much is ten thousand talents?

positions.view: Sixteen million dollars, the talent being three thousand shekels
Four and a half million sterling in silver, or sixty-seven and a half million in gold, the annual revenue of the British empire
About two and a half million sterling, named in its vague vastness rather than exactly
Ten or twelve million dollars, the talent at a thousand
One million eight hundred and seventy-five thousand pounds

debates.question: Who are the servants?

positions.view: Collectors of revenue or tributary princes, since kings farmed out a province’s taxes
Those who dispense the word, to whom that business is committed

debates.question: How far may the details of the parable be pressed?

positions.view: Not far; the selling is thrown in to keep the story consistent and explain the plea for delay
Not far; the framework was drawn from human laws and its details need not be unfolded
It would be an idle exercise of ingenuity to examine every minute clause

debates.question: What moved the remission?

positions.view: The king’s own goodness and will, not anything the man said or did
The plea answered beyond itself, so that the man is so far justified by faith
The plea was a fourfold pattern of humiliation, prayer, confidence and purpose

outliers.claim: Alone in identifying the king’s kingdom with the Son himself rather than with the Church or the Gospel dispensation.
Alone in making conscience the auditor of the reckoning, which unless bribed will not write fifty for a hundred.

28.pericope_label: The forgiven servant takes his fellow by the throat; his lord delivers him to the tormentors

schools.summary: Henry presses the comparison hard, that dishonours done to a man like ourselves are motes and gnats while dishonours done to God are talents and beams and camels, which excuses not wronging a neighbour but only our aggravating it when wronged; he asks what need there was of the violence, the debt being demandable without taking the debtor by the throat, and finds pride and malice more productive of severity than necessity, the carriage lordly and the spirit base. He holds that what gives occasion for sorrow should give occasion for prayer; and although he writes of the pardon revoked and the acquittance cancelled, at the last he will not have God reverse his pardons, only deny them to the unqualified, who had seemed humbled and thought themselves pardoned already.

Calvin refuses the Roman reading of the tormentors, calling it ridiculous to light the fire of purgatory from the word, since eternal and not temporal death is meant. Gill puts the reproof at its simplest, that it is but reasonable that such as have received mercy should show mercy.

Barnes prices the hundred pence at fourteen dollars, stops the allegory at the fellow-servants, their report being thrown in to keep the narrative consistent since God needs no informing of what his children do, and keeps the tormentors jailers, since torments were inflicted on criminals and not debtors, so that the punishment is imprisonment only. Ellicott alone resists the flattening of the smaller debt, which is no trifle but a hundred days’ wages, so that the parable grants offences between brothers may be many and grievous in themselves; he finds the creditor’s course as unwise as ungenerous, since imprisoning the debtor cuts off the very means of payment, asks whether a man really pardoned can become thus merciless and answers that the inconsistency is too fatally common, the man not consciously a hypocrite but as yet double minded, and holds that the debt may come back, faith that does not work by love ceasing to justify, the discharge traced as in sympathetic ink. Robertson lists the modern attempts at the sum from fifty shillings to twenty pounds, makes the verb inchoative, he began to throttle him, notes that Roman law allowed the indignity, renders the creditor’s words if thou owest anything, however little, calls the if a pitiless logic, observes drily that there is a limit to what people will put up with, and agrees the punishment is punitive and not purgatorial.

Clarke knows no word rendering the Greek so fully as the Anglo-saxon throttle, to half choke a man by seizing his throat, and will have the tormentors the tortures themselves, such as the Asiatics used on a suspected fraud, before turning them inward to a guilty conscience and a fearful looking for of fiery indignation. Wesley says plainly the pardon was retracted and the whole debt required, and asks whether we may still say a pardon once given can never be retracted.

debates.question: How small was the hundred pence?

positions.view: A very small sum, about fourteen dollars, to teach that offences against us are small beside ours against God
Motes and gnats beside talents and beams and camels
No trifle but a hundred days’ wages; the parable grants offences between brothers may be grievous in themselves

debates.question: Who are the tormentors?

positions.view: Keepers of the prison; torments were for criminals and not debtors, so imprisonment is all that is meant
The tortures themselves, such as the Asiatics used, and inwardly a guilty conscience
Deliberately vague: whatever agencies God employs in retribution, not avenging angels or demons
Terrible punishment, not prison simply, and punitive rather than purgatorial

debates.question: Can a pardon once granted be revoked?

positions.view: Yes; the pardon was retracted and the whole debt required
Yes; the debt may come back, and faith that does not work by love ceases to justify
No; God does not reverse his pardons but denies them to the unqualified, who only thought themselves pardoned

debates.question: Does the imprisonment support purgatory?

positions.view: No; it is ridiculous to light that fire from the word, since eternal and not temporal death is meant
No; it is punitive and not purgatorial, for he could never pay back that vast debt

outliers.claim: Alone in refusing to treat the hundred pence as trivial, making it a hundred days’ wages so that offences between brothers are granted real weight.
Alone against Wesley and Ellicott in denying that God reverses a pardon, holding instead that he denies it to those never qualified for it.
